options.text: Any device that runs on electricity
Anything designed by people to solve a problem or meet a need
Only the newest phones and computers
A material that comes directly from nature

items.explanation: Technology is anything people designed to solve a problem or meet a need. That includes a water filter or a pencil, not just electronics.

items.stem: Which of these is the best example of a technology?

options.text: A river flowing through a valley
A bridge built to cross a river

items.explanation: A bridge was designed by people to solve a problem, crossing a river. Rivers, storms, and mountains form naturally, so they are not technology.

items.stem: Smartphones let people text, video call, and share photos instantly. This shows that a technology can change
items.explanation: Instant texting and video calling changed how people communicate, one of the main ways technology reshapes daily life.

items.stem: Using machines or computers to do work that people once did by hand is called
items.explanation: Automation is using machines or computers to do work people once did by hand. It is one major way technology changes work.

items.stem: A factory builds a useful new gadget, but making it releases waste into a nearby river. The waste is an example of

options.text: an unintended effect on the environment

items.explanation: Polluting the river was not the goal of building the gadget. It is an unintended effect, and it falls on the environment.

items.stem: Why can a useful technology still create problems?

options.text: Useful technologies never cause any harm
Its benefits and its costs often come together
Problems only happen with broken technology
Costs always appear before any benefit

items.explanation: Most technologies bring benefits and costs at the same time. A technology can be genuinely useful and still cause harm, like a car that helps travel but pollutes.

items.stem: Plastic is cheap, light, and useful, but it piles up as waste that lasts for centuries. This is an example of a

options.text: trade-off between a benefit and a cost

items.explanation: A trade-off is a benefit gained in exchange for a cost. Plastic's usefulness comes with the cost of long-lasting waste.

items.stem: An engineer tests a design, learns from what fails, and redesigns it to work better. This repeating process is
items.explanation: Innovation is improving a technology through repeated cycles of testing and redesign. That is why technologies tend to get better over time.

items.stem: Which best explains why one technology, like the smartphone, changed so many parts of life at once?

options.text: Each part of society is completely separate from the others
The smartphone was used by only a few people
The parts of society are connected, so its effects spread across many of them
Technology has no effect on how people live

items.explanation: Communication, work, health, travel, and the environment are connected parts of society. A useful technology reaches many of them at once.

items.stem: Building smartphones requires mined metals, and charging them uses electricity. These facts show that technology can affect

options.text: only the people who own it
the environment, through resource and energy use

items.explanation: Mining metals and using electricity are environmental effects. A technology that helps people daily can still use resources and energy and create waste.
